children.label: Clavinet I
children.copy:
Every Hohner Clavinet we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. Unlike a Rhodes or Wurlitzer, the Clavinet doesn't use tines or reeds at all — it's built around a set of strings, dampened at rest, that are struck by rubber-tipped hammers and read by a magnetic pickup, closer in spirit to an electric guitar than a piano. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable, always working to preserve the instrument's percussive, funky character.

The Clavinet I was the very first Clavinet, introduced in 1964: a heavy, teak-veneer console instrument with a built-in amplifier and speaker, a lockable lid, and just two tablet switches for pickup selection alongside a volume control. It wasn't designed with stage use in mind — the early damping design is more prone to feedback at higher volumes than later models — but it's the instrument that started the whole Clavinet line.

children.label: Clavinet/Pianet Duo
children.copy:
Every Hohner Clavinet we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable, always working to preserve the instrument's percussive, funky character.

The Clavinet/Pianet Duo was Hohner's answer for players who wanted both instruments without hauling two separate cases: a D6-spec Clavinet and a Pianet built into a single shared cabinet, switchable between voices (and layerable, on units wired for it). Electronically it's on the same footing as the D6 and E7 — more roadworthy, quieter, and better shielded against proximity hum than the earliest Clavinets — just packaged as a true two-in-one.

children.label: Pianet N
children.copy:
Every Hohner Pianet we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. The Pianet's voice comes from a set of reeds plucked by an adhesive pad on each key rather than a hammer or tine — a simple, elegant design, but one where the pads themselves are a known wear item. Pad replacement is essentially always part of a proper Pianet restoration, and it's central to getting the responsive, even touch these instruments are known for. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable.

Designed by Ernst Zacharias and introduced in 1965, the Pianet N is the classic first-generation Pianet, built around ground stainless steel reeds, a variable-capacitance pickup, and leather-faced activation pads. It remained in production until 1977, and this same basic design covers most of the earlier Pianet variants we see come through the shop.

children.label: Pianet T
children.copy:
Every Hohner Pianet we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. The Pianet's voice comes from a set of reeds plucked by an adhesive pad on each key rather than a hammer or tine — a simple, elegant design, but one where the pads themselves are a known wear item. Pad replacement is essentially always part of a proper Pianet restoration, and it's central to getting the responsive, even touch these instruments are known for. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable.

Introduced in 1977 as Hohner moved to a new generation of Pianet design, the Pianet T replaced the Pianet N's leather-and-foam pads with molded silicone rubber pads (based on adhesive technology originally patented by NASA) plucking rolled spring-steel reeds through an electromagnetic pickup — a smoother-milled reed finish that gives the T a noticeably mellower voice than the N, though it also means Pianet T parts aren't interchangeable with earlier models.

children.label: Cembalet I
children.copy:
Every Hohner Cembalet we restore for sale goes through the same meticulous process we're known for, with dozens of hours devoted to bringing each instrument to exceptional playing condition. Designed by Ernst Zacharias and patented in 1957, the Cembalet was Hohner's first piano-like electric keyboard — built around ground stainless steel reeds read by a variable-capacitance pickup, the same core technology Zacharias would later refine into the Pianet. We prioritize period-correct vintage components whenever possible, and turn to the best available reproduction parts when originals are no longer viable, always working to preserve the instrument's original character.

The Cembalet I is the original console version, produced from the late 1950s: a 61-key instrument (C2 to C7) in a wooden cabinet with an integrated stand and basic built-in amplification, but no dedicated tonal controls.
